title: Structural crossover of complex networks: bridging degree correlation and fractality
authors: Shogo Mizutaka, Jun Yamamoto, Kousuke Yakubo
abstract: We investigate the relationship between long-range degree correlations and fractality in scale-free random networks. By analyzing degree correlations in scale-free random networks at the percolation threshold, at which a giant component emerges, we derive the ball volume $\tildeν_k(l)$, defined as the average number of nodes within distance $l$ from a root node with degree $k$. The resulting expression predicts a degree-dependent structural crossover. For $l\ll k^{1/(\df-1)}$, the ball volume grows as $\tildeν_k(l)\sim kl$, whereas for $l\gg k^{1/(\df-1)}$, it crosses over to the global fractal scaling $\tildeν_k(l)\sim l^{\df}$. Here, $\df$ is the fractal dimension of critical scale-free random networks. We further show that the structural crossover can be naturally understood in terms of critical branching processes and is also observed in empirical fractal networks.
summary: This paper analyzes the structural crossover in scale-free random networks, showing that the growth of the local volume exhibits a transition from a degree-dependent linear regime to a global fractal regime. This crossover is theoretically derived using critical branching processes and is successfully validated by applying the model to real-world biological networks.
main_problem: The paper investigates the structural crossover in complex networks, specifically bridging the relationship between long-range degree correlations and network fractality.
main_result: The average ball volume exhibits a structural crossover: $\tilde{\nu}_k(l) \sim k l$ at short distances and $\tilde{\nu}_k(l) \sim l^{D_f}$ at large distances.
method: The analysis involves deriving the ball volume $\tilde{\nu}_k(l)$ using the configuration model and relating it to critical branching processes.
model_or_system: The study focuses on scale-free random networks near the percolation threshold, and extends the findings to empirical fractal networks like protein interaction networks.
key_observables: Ball volume $\tilde{\nu}_k(l)$, structural crossover length $l_{co}(k)$, and the fractal dimension $D_f$.
important_parameters: Degree exponent $\gamma$, distance $l$, and the crossover length $l_{co}(k) \sim k^{1/(D_f-1)}$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the critical limit near the percolation threshold and assumes the network structure can be decomposed into linear and fractal components.
figures_summary: Figures show numerical confirmation of the crossover in scale-free random networks and demonstrate the linear growth term in the residual ball volume for both theoretical and empirical protein networks.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theoretical framework by deriving the ball volume $\tilde{\nu}_k(l)$ and predicting the crossover. It then confirms this prediction using critical branching process interpretations, followed by numerical verification on both synthetic scale-free graphs and real-world biological networks.
why_interesting: While focused on network theory, the concept of structural crossover governed by scaling laws and critical phenomena is highly relevant to understanding phase transitions and connectivity in complex quantum systems or disordered quantum materials.
